full_judgment:
Mr. A.N.M. Bashir Ullah, J:- This Rule, on an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the CPC) filed by the pre-emptee-petitioners calling upon the opposite party no. I to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 14.07.2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Jessore in Miscellaneous Appeal No.56 of 2010 affirming the order dated 26/09/2010 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.80 of 2005 by the learned Assistant Judge, Monirampur, Jessore shall not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the opposite-party No.1 Sree Uttam Kumar Sarker as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.80 of 2005 under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (in short, the Act) in the Court of Assistant Judge, Monirampur, Jessore for pre-emption of the case land sold by a kabala dated 21.09.2005. When the said proceeding was matured for hearing, the opposite-party Nos. l and 2 of the said proceeding (the present-petitioners) filed an application for local investigation of the case land in order to determine whether the petitioner and the contesting opposite party Nos. I and 2 have been living in separate homestead having separate gate for their entrance and divided by a common wall. The trial Court by its order dated 26.9.2010 rejected the said petition and against the said order the opposite-party Nos. I and 2 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.80 of 2005 in the Court of learned District Judge, Jessore and the appeal was ultimately heard by the Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Jessore who by his impugned judgment and order dated 14.7.2011 dismissed the appeal. The pre-emptee-opposite-party Nos. 1 and 2 being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with said judgment and order moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. The Rule is resisted by the pre-emptor opposite-party No. 1. 

 6. On the other hand, Mr. Surojit Battacharjee, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite-party No.1 opposes the Rule. He submits that in deciding fate of the pre-emption proceeding under discussion it is not at all material whether the petitioner and the opposite-party Nos.1 and 2 of the original proceeding have been living in separate homestead, whether they have any separate entrance and whether there was a common wall between them. The only points that needs to be decided in a proceeding like this whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer for the case land and to address the said point local investigation was not at all necessary. The whole attention and attitude of the opposite-party Nos.1 and 2 was nothing but to drag the trial of the 

 10. From the petition filed by the opposite-party Nos.1 and 2 (the present petitioners) for local investigation it appears that to, address some facts whether the case land is 111 required for the petitioner for maintaining his privacy he sought the local investigation. Section 24 of the Act provides no scope for filing a case for pre-emption of any land for maintaining privacy rather section 24 has provided the provisions that if a portion or share of the Non-Agricultural land held by a Non-Agricultural tenant is transferred one or more co-sharer tenants of such land may apply to the Court for such portion or share to he transferred to himself or themselves. So in deciding a proceeding under section 24 of the Act, the Court is to consider whether the applicant is the co-sharer for the case land. Since the maintenance of the privacy is not the requirements of the law in a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Act there cannot he any local investigation on such a issue which is not a legal issue at all. 

 14. However, be that as it may I find no minimum justification for filing a petition for local investigation to ascertain whether the petitioner and the opposite-party Nos.1 and 2 have been living in the separate homestead having separate gate for their entrance divided by a common wall. The only point that requires to be ascertained in such a proceeding whether the petitioner is a co-sharer for the case land along with some other requirement as provided in the law. So I had no merit in the Rule. The Courts below did not commit any error of law in rejecting the petition for local investigation occasioning any failure of justice to the petitioners.
